tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

One to three lines per bullet. No narrative paragraphs, no speculation, no secrets.

area.description: Optional short tag naming the part of Claude Code this is about (e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing"). Leave blank if unclear.

failure_mode.description: When the report is about MODEL BEHAVIOR (not a product bug), the closest failure mode, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value. Omit only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

The server reads the live index.html, applies every edit in order, and publishes the result as one new version; if any edit cannot be applied, nothing is published. tools.name: mcp__claude-artifacts__read_artifact
tools.description: Read the current document of an artifact: one that the user owns, or one that belongs to someone in the user's organization and that the user can open. Read a pasted claude.ai artifact link with this tool. Returns a JSON summary (slug, version id, title, favicon, runtime-contract version, total_lines, and for a multi-file artifact its file names), then the HTML of the version the user is served, then a reminder. The HTML, and the summary's title, favicon and file names, are wrapped in an <untrusted-document-...> tag that the summary's notice names; the tag is not part of them. A document over ~1 MiB is not served whole: read it in parts with offset and limit, which count lines; next_offset says where the next part starts. A part is a piece of the document: never send one to publish_version as the whole page. Artifacts that contain a live (collaboratively edited) document are not served. For a multi-file artifact only the entry document (index.html) is returned. Use this tool before republishing an artifact: change the page with edit_version, or send the whole edited HTML to publish_version, with base_version set to the returned version. Use read_shared_artifact instead for an artifact in the user's organization that the user does not own and that an agent or a Coworker owns, can write to or has written to, or that someone outside that organization has written to. An artifact made from a type is not served either, and read_shared_artifact shows at most the type's page: for one the user owns, start with list_files, if this server offers it. After read_artifact answers not found, do not try read_shared_artifact: it answers the same. read_artifact serves the live version of an artifact the user can edit, otherwise the version shared with the user.

1	"""Summarize message labels in a CSV file and save a run report."""
2	
3	import argparse
4	import csv
5	import hashlib
6	import io
7	import json
8	from pathlib import Path
9	import platform
10	import sys
11	
12	
13	def describe(input_path):
14	    raw = input_path.read_bytes()
15	    rows = csv.DictReader(io.StringIO(raw.decode("utf-8"), newline=""))
16	    if rows.fieldnames != ["message_id", "text", "label"]:
17	        raise ValueError("Expected columns: message_id,text,label.")
18	
19	    counts = {"ham": 0, "spam": 0}
20	    seen_ids = set()
21	    for number, row in enumerate(rows, start=1):
22	        if None in row or any(not value or not value.strip() for value in row.values()):
23	            raise ValueError(f"Record {number}: missing or extra field.")
24	        if row["message_id"] in seen_ids:
25	            raise ValueError(f"Record {number}: duplicate message_id.")
26	        if row["label"] not in counts:
27	            raise ValueError(f"Record {number}: label must be ham or spam.")
28	        seen_ids.add(row["message_id"])
29	        counts[row["label"]] += 1
30	
31	    if not seen_ids:
32	        raise ValueError("The file contains no messages.")
33	
34	    return {
35	        "input_file": str(input_path.resolve()),
36	        "input_sha256": hashlib.sha256(raw).hexdigest(),
37	        "total_messages": sum(counts.values()),
38	        "label_counts": counts,
39	        "runtime": {
40	            "python_executable": sys.executable,
41	            "python_version": platform.python_version(),
42	            "working_directory": str(Path.cwd()),
43	        },
44	    }
45	
46	
47	def main():
48	    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
49	    parser.add_argument("--data", type=Path, required=True, help="Input CSV file")
50	    parser.add_argument("--out", type=Path, required=True, help="Output JSON report")
51	    args = parser.parse_args()
52	    if args.data.resolve() == args.out.resolve():
53	        parser.error("The report must be a different file from the input data.")
54	
55	    try:
56	        report = describe(args.data)
57	        args.out.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
58	        args.out.write_text(
59	            json.dumps(report, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2) + "\n", encoding="utf-8"
60	        )
61	    except (OSError, UnicodeError, csv.Error, ValueError) as error:
62	        parser.exit(1, f"Error: {error}\n")
63	
64	    print(f"Report saved: {args.out.resolve()}")
65	    print(f"Messages: {report['total_messages']}; labels: {report['label_counts']}")
66	
67	
68	if __name__ == "__main__":
69	    main()
70

# Data for the first run

## Field definitions

| CSV field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `message_id` | Identifier within this packet; links to `raw/<message_id>.eml`. |
| `text` | Decoded subject (`Subject:`), a blank line, and the full message body. |
| `label` | Source dataset label: `spam` or `ham` (legitimate email). |

The label is not produced by our script. Do not infer it from a single word: a legitimate email can contain an advertising footer. One CSV record can span multiple lines because the text retains its paragraph breaks.

## Sources and preparation

Source: [Apache SpamAssassin public corpus](https://spamassassin.apache.org/old/publiccorpus/), archives [20030228_easy_ham.tar.bz2](https://spamassassin.apache.org/old/publiccorpus/20030228_easy_ham.tar.bz2) and [20030228_spam.tar.bz2](https://spamassassin.apache.org/old/publiccorpus/20030228_spam.tar.bz2). Prepared on 2026-10-22. The data is included locally; students do not need to download it.

Short, single-part `text/plain` messages were selected for manual inspection. This is not a random or representative sample for training or evaluating a filter. `demo.csv` and `exercise.csv` contain different messages. This historical corpus does not represent present-day email.

Transformations:

1. The selected archive members were preserved byte for byte in `raw/`, with new filenames matching `message_id`. These are originals **from the published corpus**, whose publisher had already modified some addresses and hostnames.
2. Python's standard-library `email` parser read each message using `policy.default`. The subject, body transfer encoding, and declared character encoding were decoded (ASCII when no charset was declared). Line endings were normalized to LF. Bodies were not truncated; quotations and footers were retained.
3. The `text` field was assembled as `Subject: <subject>`, two newlines, and the body. Other headers remain in the original `.eml` file, but are not included in the CSV.
4. Labels came from the archive directory: `easy_ham` → `ham`, `spam` → `spam`. Local identifiers were assigned, and the CSV files were saved as UTF-8 with LF line endings.

`manifest.json` records archive URLs and SHA-256 hashes, selected archive members, their `.eml` paths, and hashes of the originals and CSV packets. It supports reproducing the selection and checking it against the same archives. Filenames, identifiers, and labels are not input features for the future model.

## Usage terms

According to the [corpus description](https://spamassassin.apache.org/old/publiccorpus/readme.html), copyright in the message texts remains with the original senders. The SpamAssassin software license is not a license for these messages. The publisher instructs users not to send them through a live email system. In this project, we read files as text; we do not send the messages or open their links.

content.text:
Przeczytałem `README.md`, `describe_data.py` oraz `data/README.md`, bo główny README odsyła tam po definicje pól. Niczego nie uruchamiałem ani nie zmieniałem. Wylistowałem tylko katalogi i podejrzałem początek `data/exercise.csv`. Katalog `results/` jeszcze nie istnieje.

## Co skrypt czyta

**Wejście:** jeden plik CSV podany w `--data` (wymagany argument, `describe_data.py:49`).

- Czyta surowe bajty pliku i dekoduje je jako UTF-8 (`describe_data.py:14-15`).
- Parsuje je przez `csv.DictReader`. Ten parser obsługuje pola w cudzysłowach, które ciągną się przez wiele linii. Dlatego skrypt liczy rekordy, a nie fizyczne linie.
- Sprawdza dane i przy pierwszym błędzie przerywa działanie:
  - nagłówek musi brzmieć dokładnie `message_id,text,label` (`:16-17`),
  - żadne pole nie może być puste ani nadmiarowe (`:22-23`),
  - `message_id` nie może się powtarzać (`:24-25`),
  - `label` musi mieć wartość `ham` albo `spam` (`:26-27`),
  - plik musi zawierać co najmniej jedną wiadomość (`:31-32`).

Według README zamierzone wejście to `data/exercise.csv` (krok 3, linia 31).

## Co skrypt zapisuje

**Wyjście:** raport JSON w ścieżce z `--out` (`:50`). Zamierzona ścieżka według README to `results/exercise-summary.json` (linia 31).

- Jeśli katalog docelowy nie istnieje, skrypt go tworzy (`:57`). Istniejący raport nadpisuje (`:58`).
- Odmawia działania, gdy `--out` wskazuje ten sam plik co `--data` (`:52-53`).
- Raport zawiera te pola (`:34-44`):
  - `input_file`: bezwzględna ścieżka do wejścia,
  - `input_sha256`: suma kontrolna bajtów wejścia,
  - `total_messages`: liczba rekordów,
  - `label_counts`: liczby etykiet `ham` i `spam`,
  - `runtime`: ścieżka interpretera, wersja Pythona i katalog roboczy.
- Na standardowe wyjście wypisuje dwie linie: ścieżkę zapisanego raportu oraz liczby wiadomości i etykiet (`:64-65`).
- Przy błędzie danych lub pliku kończy z kodem 1 i komunikatem `Error: ...`, a raportu nie zapisuje (`:61-62`). Stary raport może jednak nadal leżeć na dysku.

## Fragmenty README, na których się opieram

- **Linia 3:** program tylko liczy istniejące etykiety. Nie trenuje modelu i nie uruchamia filtra SpamAssassin.
- **Linia 9 (tabela plików):** „Read a CSV, count messages and labels, and save a JSON report.”
- **Linia 18:** jeden rekord to jeden e-mail, a `text` może zajmować wiele linii. „Counting physical lines in the CSV does not count messages.”
- **Linie 31 i 34:** komenda z intended input/output. Skrypt sam tworzy katalog wyjściowy, a kolejne uruchomienie z tym samym `--out` nadpisuje raport.
- **Linie 45-48 (sekcja „Reading the report”):** znaczenie pól raportu, zgodne z kodem.
- **Linia 50:** błąd kończy program z niezerowym kodem wyjścia, a samo istnienie raportu nie dowodzi, że ostatnie uruchomienie się powiodło. Zgadza się to z `parser.exit(1, ...)` w kodzie.

## Przykładowa wiadomość z `data/exercise.csv`

Pierwszy rekord, dokładnie w takiej postaci, w jakiej jest zapisany w pliku:

```
exercise-001,"Subject: [SAdev] Interesting approach to Spam handling..

Hello, have you seen and discussed this article and his approach?

Thank you

http://www.paulgraham.com/spam.html
-- ""Hell, there are no rules here-- we're trying to accomplish something.""
-- Thomas Alva Edison




-------------------------------------------------------
This sf.net email is sponsored by: OSDN - Tired of that same old
cell phone?  Get a new here for FREE!
https://www.inphonic.com/r.asp?r=sourceforge1&refcode1=vs3390
_______________________________________________
Spamassassin-devel mailing list
Spamassassin-devel@lists.sourceforge.net
https://lists.sourceforge.net/lists/listinfo/spamassassin-devel

",ham
```

**Pola** (definicje z `data/README.md:7-9`):

- **`message_id`** = `exercise-001`. To identyfikator nadany lokalnie w tym zestawie danych. Łączy rekord z oryginalną wiadomością w pliku `data/raw/exercise-001.eml`, w którym są też pozostałe nagłówki e-maila. Skrypt sprawdza tylko, czy identyfikator jest niepusty i unikalny.
- **`text`** = wszystko w cudzysłowie: linia `Subject: ...`, pusta linia, a potem pełna treść wiadomości. Pole zajmuje wiele fizycznych linii, ale to nadal jeden rekord. Podwójny cudzysłów `""` to sposób zapisu znaku `"` wewnątrz pola CSV, więc po wczytaniu jest to zwykły cudzysłów. Skrypt nie analizuje treści, sprawdza tylko, czy pole nie jest puste.
- **`label`** = `ham`, czyli wiadomość prawidłowa według zbioru źródłowego. Etykieta pochodzi z katalogu archiwum SpamAssassin (`easy_ham` → `ham`) i nie jest wynikiem działania skryptu, który ją tylko liczy.

Ten przykład dobrze ilustruje ostrzeżenie z `data/README.md:11`: wiadomość ma reklamową stopkę („Get a new here for FREE!”), a mimo to jest oznaczona jako `ham`. Etykiety nie należy więc wnioskować z pojedynczych słów.

## Pojęcia, które mogą być nowe

- **ham / spam:** e-mail chciany / niechciany.
- **SHA-256:** suma kontrolna, czyli „odcisk palca” pliku. Pozwala sprawdzić, czy dwie wersje pliku są identyczne, ale nie mówi nic o poprawności danych.
- **kod wyjścia (exit status):** liczba zwracana przez program. 0 oznacza sukces, każda inna wartość oznacza błąd.

Następny krok według README to sprawdzenie katalogu roboczego i wersji Pythona (`py -3 --version`), a potem uruchomienie komendy z kroku 3.

## Jak `describe_data.py` liczy wiadomości

Przykładowy plik CSV:

```
message_id,text,label
m1,"Subject: Hello

Line one
Line two",ham
m2,"Subject: WIN NOW

Click here",spam
```

Ten plik ma 7 fizycznych linii, ale tylko **2 rekordy**. Skrypt przetwarza go tak:

1. Wczytuje bajty i dekoduje je jako UTF-8. Gdyby plik nie był poprawnym UTF-8, skończyłby się błąd `UnicodeError`.
2. `csv.DictReader` czyta pierwszą linię jako nagłówek. Musi to być dokładnie `["message_id", "text", "label"]`.
3. Treść w cudzysłowie to jedno pole, nawet jeśli zawiera znaki nowej linii albo przecinki. Dlatego `m1` i `m2` to po jednym rekordzie.
4. Każdy rekord przechodzi kontrole i zwiększa licznik swojej etykiety.

Wynik: `total_messages: 2`, `label_counts: {"ham": 1, "spam": 1}`. Raport zostaje zapisany, a kod wyjścia to 0.

## Kiedy skrypt kończy się błędem

Skrypt zatrzymuje się na **pierwszym** problemie. Wtedy:
- wypisuje `Error: ...`,
- kończy z kodem wyjścia **1**,
- **nie zapisuje** raportu (stary raport, jeśli był, zostaje na dysku).

| Sytuacja | Komunikat |
|---|---|
| Inny nagłówek, np. `id,text,label` albo inna kolejność kolumn | `Expected columns: message_id,text,label.` |
| Brakujące pole, puste pole, pole z samych spacji albo nadmiarowe pole | `Record N: missing or extra field.` |
| Powtórzony `message_id` | `Record N: duplicate message_id.` |
| Etykieta inna niż dokładnie `ham` albo `spam` | `Record N: label must be ham or spam.` |
| Same nagłówki, bez rekordów | `The file contains no messages.` |
| `--out` wskazuje ten sam plik co `--data` | błąd argumentów, kod wyjścia 2 |

`N` to numer **rekordu**, liczony od 1 bez nagłówka, a nie numer linii w pliku.

## Twoja kolej: zmieniony przypadek

```
message_id,text,label
m1,"Subject: Lunch

See you at noon, Bob",ham
m2,"Subject: Offer
Buy now",spam
m3,"Subject: Re: Lunch

Thanks",Ham
```

"""Check a saved report using three synthetic messages: two ham and one spam."""

import json
from pathlib import Path
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
import unittest


PROJECT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
FIXTURE = PROJECT / "tests" / "fixtures" / "messages.csv"


class ReportTest(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_cli_writes_expected_counts(self):
        """The CLI saves a report for the intended input with counts 3 / 2 / 1."""
        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix="spam-lab-test-") as directory:
            output = Path(directory) / "summary.json"
            result = subprocess.run(
                [sys.executable, str(PROJECT / "describe_data.py"),
                 "--data", str(FIXTURE), "--out", str(output)],
                cwd=PROJECT,
                capture_output=True,
                text=True,
            )
            self.assertEqual(result.returncode, 0, result.stdout + result.stderr)
            self.assertTrue(output.is_file(), "The program did not save a report.")
            report = json.loads(output.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
            self.assertEqual(report["input_file"], str(FIXTURE))
            self.assertEqual(report["total_messages"], 3)
            self.assertEqual(report["label_counts"], {"ham": 2, "spam": 1})


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main()

Raport dla `data/exercise.csv` powstał w `results\exercise-summary.json` i zawiera 8 wiadomości: 5 `ham` i 3 `spam`. Test z README też przeszedł. Kod, dane i testy są niezmienione, niczego nie instalowałem.

## Przebieg

**1. Środowisko**
```
PS> Get-Location; py -3 --version; "exit code: $LASTEXITCODE"

Python 3.13.1 spełnia wymóg wersji co najmniej 3.10.

**2. Stan przed uruchomieniem**

`Test-Path results` zwróciło `False` i `Test-Path results\exercise-summary.json` też `False`. Raportu wcześniej nie było, więc ten plik powstał w tym uruchomieniu.

Żeby to wyjaśnić, przeczytałem `tests/test_report.py` i `tests/fixtures/messages.csv`.

**Dane:** `tests/fixtures/messages.csv` zawiera 3 syntetyczne wiadomości, które nie pochodzą ze SpamAssassin: `test-001` (ham), `test-002` (spam) i `test-003` (ham). exercise-004,"Subject: [ILUG] Re: Problems with RAID1 on cobalt raq3

On Mon, Aug 19, 2002 at 03:08:16PM +0100, John P. Looney mentioned:
>  This is likely because to get it to boot, like the cobalt, I'm actually
> passing root=/dev/hda5 to the kernel, not /dev/md0. 

 Just to solve this...the reason I was booting the box with
root=/dev/hda5, not /dev/md0 was because /dev/md0 wasn't booting - it
would barf with 'can't find init'.

 It turns out that this is because I was populating md0 with tar. Which
seems to have 'issues' with crosslinked files - for instance, it was
trying to make a hard link of glibc.so to hda - and failing. It was only
as I did it again with a friend present, that he spotted the errors, and
queried them. We noticed that the hard linked files just didn't exist on
the new rootfs.

 When we duplicated the filesystems with dump instead of tar, it worked
fine, I was able to tell lilo to use root=/dev/md0 and everything worked.

 Woohoo.

Kate

**Porównanie raportu z przewidywaniem.** Słusznie. Warto porównać wszystkie pola, nie tylko liczebności, czyli też `input_sha256`, `input_file` i `runtime`.
